sections.html:
• Origin: Burma, Sumatra, Thailand
  • Social: peaceful schooling fish
  • Tank level: all
  • Minimum tank size: 20 gallons (about 75 litres)
  • Diet: omnivore, eats most foods
  • Breeding: egglayer
  • Life expectancy: 5 years

This easy-going species is hardy, simple to care for, and compatible with most other peaceful fish. It makes an excellent beginner fish and breeds easily in captivity.

The name should not be confused with the celestial pearl danio, also known as the galaxy rasbora, Danio margaritatus, which is a dark-colored danio with red or orange fins and white spots on the body.

First imported to Europe in 1911, this species has been popular in the aquarium trade ever since. It originates from clear, swiftly moving streams and rivers in Myanmar (formerly Burma), Thailand, and Sumatra.

The fish has several scientific names, a few of which were assigned to what were later determined to be colour variants of the same species. Debate still exists over the classification of these colour differences. At one time the species was placed in the genus Brachydanio, which has since been declared invalid. The name Danio albolineatus means white-lined danio.
In nature, they live in clear, fast-moving streams and rivers and feed primarily on insects and zooplankton.
Pearl danios thrive in a minimum of a 20-gallon tank (about 75 litres) due to their need for ample swimming space. Longer tanks are preferable, with plants along the back and sides.

Originating from fast-moving streams and rivers, the pearl danio is accustomed to strong water currents. Because they require a slightly higher oxygen level than other danios, good filtration is important. They swim at all levels, but due to their propensity for jumping, the tank should be well covered.

Their iridescent colours are most visible under reflected, overhead lighting, and they are particularly fond of early-morning sunlight.

Temperature 18 to 24 °C (64 to 75 °F), pH 6.5 to 7.0, hardness 5 to 12 dGH. Pearl danios tolerate colder temperatures well and may even be kept in an unheated aquarium. Although undemanding about water parameters, they do best in neutral (pH 7.0) water that is soft to slightly hard.

Pearl danios accept all types of live, frozen, and flake food. In nature, their diet consists primarily of insects and zooplankton. To maintain health, feed good quality tropical flake or granulated food, as well as frozen and live foods such as tubifex, mosquito larvae, brine shrimp, and daphnia.

Pearl danios are peaceful and well suited to community aquariums, getting along with any peaceful fish. They tolerate a wide range of water conditions, which also makes them suited to combining with a variety of other fish. Like other danios, they live in schools and should be kept in groups of at least five to eight, and preferably more. Males show their best colours if at least one female is present.

Male and female pearl danios are similar in appearance. The biggest difference is that, when full of eggs, the female has a more rounded body shape. Females are larger overall and fuller-bodied. Males are smaller, slimmer, and more brightly coloured, and often show a red tint along the underside.

The pearl danio has a pearly, blue-violet body with an orange-red stripe extending from the tail to mid-body, a forked tail and two sets of paired barbels. In some areas a yellow-ochre variant called the yellow danio can be found.

Pearl danios are an easy-to-breed egg-laying fish. As with other danios, breeding pairs are very loyal. The breeding tank should be warm, 26 to 30 °C (79 to 86 °F), with a shallow water level of about 10 to 15 cm. Provide fine-leaved plants, either floating or planted in a group. Marbles make an excellent substrate that lets stray eggs fall out of reach of the adults. A breeding grid or mop on the bottom would also protect the eggs.

They spawn as pairs or in a school. Place half as many females as males in the breeding tank several days before introducing the males. Once the males are added, pairs form and leave the group to scatter eggs.

Spawning can also be triggered by adding a small amount of water every few hours so the tank is gradually topped up, simulating the rainy season. Pairs spawn the next morning; a spawned female is noticeably slimmer. Remove the adults as soon as spawning is finished, otherwise they will eat the eggs.

Keep the tank dark while the eggs develop to prevent fungal growth. The fry emerge in 36 to 48 hours and should be fed freshly hatched brine shrimp or infusoria. Young danios grow rapidly and are free-swimming in six to seven days. Fry may be raised on finely ground dry food or commercial fry food.
